paragraphs: Online continual learning trains a network as changing data arrive, with only one pass through the incoming stream. Rehearsal methods keep a small memory of older examples and revisit them to reduce forgetting. The paper examines why this can still fail: a small memory may poorly represent how prediction error behaves across the full set of past data.

The authors analyze rehearsal as an optimization problem whose training sample is both biased and changing. Their analysis highlights a tension: too little rehearsal leaves past knowledge insufficiently learned, while excessive repetition risks fitting the memory too closely. Repeated Augmented Rehearsal combines repeated practice with data augmentation to address both sides of this problem.

Across four benchmarks, the method improves on ordinary rehearsal by 9–17% and also strengthens MIR, ASER, and SCR. The authors report better approximation of past-data loss and learning trajectories that avoid high-loss ridges. They additionally study how repetition and augmentation interact, and use reinforcement learning to adjust settings as the balance between retaining knowledge and learning new information changes.
neurips-2022-a-simple-but-strong-baselin.tldr: Repeated Augmented Rehearsal combines repetition and augmentation to improve learning from changing data while reducing forgetting.

paragraphs: Score-based query attacks repeatedly inspect a model's output scores to work out which input changes will cause a mistake. This paper targets the information those scores provide to the attacker. Its central observation is that small disturbances to the apparent loss trend can send an attack in the wrong direction.

Adversarial Attack on Attackers, or AAA, slightly modifies the model's output logits after prediction. The modification is designed to confuse the greedy search strategy used by score-based attacks while largely preserving the original predictions. The defense therefore works through the attacker's feedback rather than requiring an improvement in the underlying model's worst-case robustness. The authors also report improved confidence calibration without reduced clean accuracy.

In one reported CIFAR-10 experiment, WideResNet-28 with AAA achieves 80.59% accuracy under a 2,500-query Square attack, compared with 67.44% for adversarial training, at an infinity-norm bound of 8/255. Broader experiments compare eight defenses across eight models and six score-based attacks. These findings support the proposed mechanism across the tested attack configurations.
neurips-2022-adversarial-attack-on-attac.tldr: AAA modifies output scores to misdirect score-based adversarial attacks while preserving clean accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In combinatorial semi-bandits, a decision can involve several arms, including arms activated probabilistically by that decision. The paper studies how learning performance depends on K, the maximum number pulled or triggered in a round. Its target is regret: the accumulated performance shortfall associated with learning which choices work best.

For probabilistically triggered arms, the authors introduce a condition that accounts for both triggering probabilities and variability. Under this condition, their BCUCB-T algorithm uses confidence intervals that reflect variance. The analysis reduces a linear dependence on K to a logarithmic or squared-logarithmic dependence. The condition applies to settings including cascading bandits, network exploration, and influence maximization.

For independent arms without probabilistic triggering, the authors develop SESCB using a corresponding version of the condition. Here, the leading regret term has no dependence on K. The analysis also sharpens several existing results by a logarithmic factor. Experiments report improvements over benchmark algorithms, complementing the theoretical distinction between reduced batch-size dependence in the triggered setting and its removal from the leading term in the independent setting.
neurips-2022-batch-size-independent-regr.tldr: New conditions and algorithms reduce batch-size dependence in semi-bandit regret bounds, eliminating it from the leading term for independent, non-triggered arms.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning lets multiple workers train collaboratively while communicating through a sparse graph. This paper considers workers sampling from the same dataset or data distribution. It asks why established theory does not adequately explain which communication patterns work well or why collaboration can support larger learning rates.

The authors identify two mismatches between theory and observed behavior. The graph's spectral gap does not reliably predict empirical deep-learning performance. Existing theory also recommends smaller learning rates as graphs grow, despite the practical benefit of combining workers' information to obtain more accurate gradients. This creates a particularly stark difficulty when trying to explain convergence on infinite graphs.

The paper analyzes how graph topology affects convergence in a quadratic example, then develops results for smooth convex and strongly convex objectives. The resulting theory matches reported deep-learning observations and describes the relative performance of different graph structures. Its contribution is a more informative account of communication topology in the shared-distribution setting, connecting mathematical analysis with the practical benefits of collaborative optimization.
neurips-2022-beyond-spectral-gap-the-rol.tldr: The paper develops a topology-sensitive account of decentralized optimization that better matches observed benefits when workers share a data distribution.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields can represent scenes for realistic rendering, but their implicit structure makes editing and combining objects difficult. This paper introduces a representation designed to support those operations while also allowing flexible compression. It represents the scene through a hybrid tensor rank decomposition learned without neural networks.

The central training idea is to concentrate the most important scene information in lower ranks of the decomposition. Inspired by low-rank approximation in singular value decomposition, the rank-residual strategy makes later rank truncation useful: removing components reduces storage and detail without requiring another optimization stage. The authors describe the resulting compression as near-optimal.

The same representation supports composition by concatenating models along the rank dimension after transforming them. Objects that matter less in the combined scene can receive stronger compression, limiting storage growth. The reported rendering quality is comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The practical contribution is therefore a scene representation whose structure supports a controllable tradeoff between detail and size, together with convenient assembly of multiple models.
neurips-2022-compressible-composable-ner.tldr: A rank-based scene representation enables compression and composition while maintaining rendering quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses historical data to learn better decisions. Different algorithms and hyperparameter settings can produce policies with substantially different performance, so choosing among them is part of the learning problem. This paper addresses that choice when data are scarce and the selection process itself must rely entirely on historical records.

The authors propose a pipeline for training, comparing, selecting, and deploying policies across tasks and learning methods. Drawing on statistical model selection, it emphasizes using multiple data splits. With a small dataset, the particular split can strongly affect which candidate appears best; repeating the splitting process aims to make the selection more reliable.

Across simulated healthcare, education, and robotics settings, the pipeline produces higher-performing deployed policies than the alternative approaches evaluated. The experiments include a broad range of offline policy-learning algorithms. These results make the case that improving the selection procedure can improve the eventual policy, even without introducing a new underlying learning algorithm. The work moves toward automated algorithm and hyperparameter selection for offline reinforcement learning.
neurips-2022-data-efficient-pipeline-for.tldr: A historical-data-only selection pipeline uses multiple data splits to choose better offline reinforcement-learning policies when datasets are small.

paragraphs: In a two-sided matching market, agents must discover which firms they prefer while competing with other agents for matches. Feedback is noisy, and an agent's ability to interact with a firm depends on that competition. The paper develops decentralized algorithms for reaching stable matches in markets with structured preferences.

Each agent makes decisions using only its own history of play. The algorithms require neither communication and coordination among agents nor advance knowledge of firms' preferences. Their design separates two difficulties: statistically learning preferences from noisy observations and managing competition for firms. This separation allows learning to proceed using locally available information.

Under structural assumptions on agent and firm preferences, the authors prove that regret grows at most logarithmically with the time horizon. This establishes favorable long-run learning behavior for the markets covered by those assumptions. However, the same regret can grow exponentially with market size in the worst case. The result therefore distinguishes efficiency over time from scalability across increasingly large markets, rather than treating them as interchangeable guarantees.
neurips-2022-decentralized-communication.tldr: Agents can learn stable matches from their own histories with logarithmic time-dependent regret under structural assumptions, although worst-case market-size dependence can be exponential.

paragraphs: Temporal action segmentation assigns action labels over time. A useful prediction must capture both the actions present and their temporal relationships. This paper introduces Differentiable Temporal Logic, or DTL, as a way to incorporate temporal constraints into deep networks through their training loss.

DTL interprets a network's outputs as truth assignments for a temporal logic formula. It then computes a loss measuring how well those outputs agree with the specified constraints. The authors develop a collection of constraints that are implicit in existing annotations and incorporate them through this mechanism. Because the framework is model-agnostic, the same general approach can be used with different task models.

In temporal action segmentation experiments, adding DTL improves performance and reduces logical errors across the evaluated models. The paper also provides visual analysis of the effects on predictions. These findings suggest that temporal relationships contained in annotations can serve as useful training information beyond individual action labels. The contribution is a differentiable connection between explicit temporal rules and the output behavior of learned models.
neurips-2022-don-t-pour-cereal-into-coff.tldr: Differentiable Temporal Logic turns temporal constraints into a training loss that improves action segmentation and reduces logical errors.

paragraphs: Creating useful reinforcement-learning environments requires substantial engineering work beyond designing learning algorithms. Procedural generation adds further complexity because environments must produce varied situations for testing robustness and generalization. GriddlyJS addresses this development burden with a browser-based environment built on the Griddly engine.

The tool supports designing and debugging complex grid-world environments with procedural content. Researchers can also visualize, evaluate, and record trained agents within the same workflow. Its use of web capabilities makes it possible to publish interactive demonstrations that reproduce experimental results directly in a browser, addressing difficulties associated with complex environment build processes.

The authors demonstrate the tool by developing a compositional puzzle-solving environment, alongside human-designed configurations and their solutions. These examples support uses in automatic curriculum learning and offline reinforcement learning. The contribution is an open-source environment-development and demonstration workflow, with the puzzle task illustrating its versatility. By connecting environment construction, agent inspection, and interactive publication, GriddlyJS aims to make the supporting infrastructure of reinforcement-learning research easier to create and share.
neurips-2022-griddlyjs-a-web-ide-for-rei.tldr: GriddlyJS provides browser-based tools for building reinforcement-learning grid worlds, evaluating agents, and sharing interactive experimental demonstrations.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement-learning methods requires environments that expose different strengths and weaknesses. In tabular settings, where states and actions are represented explicitly, the paper identifies a lack of standard benchmark selection grounded in the theory of environmental difficulty. Its goal is to make that theory useful for practical evaluation.

The authors survey theoretical measures of hardness and introduce Colosseum, a package for empirical analysis. Its benchmark includes environments chosen to vary across different hardness measures. The paper also studies computable measures experimentally and evaluates five tabular agents, connecting theoretical descriptions of difficulty with observed learning behavior.

The authors extend the empirical evaluation to four agents using non-tabular versions of Colosseum environments. Those results demonstrate that tabular hardness measures can have relevance beyond their original setting. At the same time, the paper explicitly recognizes that stronger theoretical understanding of non-tabular difficulty remains needed. The contribution is a principled starting point for benchmark design, together with software and experiments that help researchers examine what makes particular environments challenging.
neurips-2022-hardness-in-markov-decision.tldr: Colosseum connects reinforcement-learning hardness theory with diverse benchmarks and empirical analysis of agent performance.

paragraphs: Generating human motion inside a 3D scene requires connecting an action to the surrounding objects and to a goal. The paper argues that existing human-scene interaction datasets offer insufficient scale, quality, and semantic information for this challenge. It introduces HUMANISE, a synthetic dataset built to connect motion, scene geometry, and language.

The dataset is constructed by aligning captured human motion sequences with different indoor scenes. The aligned motions receive automatically generated descriptions that identify both the action and the particular object involved. This makes the language more specific than a general action label: it can distinguish which object in the scene a person should interact with.

Using this dataset, the authors define a task in which a model generates motion conditioned jointly on a scene and a language instruction. Their generative model aims to produce the requested action with the specified object. Experiments demonstrate diverse motions that are consistent with the intended semantics. The work contributes both the data needed to study this joint task and a model showing how the three information sources can be combined.
neurips-2022-humanise-language-condition.tldr: HUMANISE pairs motion, indoor scenes, and language to support generating diverse human movements involving specified objects.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many observations are needed to determine whether binary variables are mutually independent. More precisely, a tester must distinguish a product distribution from a distribution at least epsilon away from every product distribution in total variation distance. For arbitrary distributions over n binary variables, this task requires exponentially many samples.

The authors show that a structural restriction changes the sample requirement substantially. They assume the distribution is Markov with respect to a Bayesian network whose directed acyclic graph has at most d incoming edges per node. Under this bounded-degree assumption, they establish a necessary and sufficient sample complexity of approximately 2^(d/2) times n divided by epsilon squared, up to logarithmic factors.

For fixed d, this gives essentially linear dependence on the number of variables, rather than the exponential dependence of the unrestricted problem. The dependence on d also makes clear how the guarantee changes as the allowed network structure becomes richer. By providing both upper and lower bounds, the paper characterizes the statistical difficulty of independence testing for this structured class.
neurips-2022-independence-testing-for-bo.tldr: Bounded-degree Bayesian-network structure reduces independence testing to essentially linear sample complexity in the number of variables when the degree is fixed.

paragraphs: Neural models of atomic interactions can learn from accurate quantum-mechanical calculations, but producing those training labels is expensive. Traditional empirical interatomic potentials offer cheaper, physically motivated approximations. This paper asks how knowledge from those older models can improve neural networks when accurate labeled data are insufficient.

The authors propose two strategies that exploit otherwise unlabeled examples. The first uses an auxiliary classifier to select a suitable empirical potential, whose energy estimates supplement the accurate density-functional-theory labels during training. The second first trains the neural network on a large collection of inexpensive empirical-potential energies, then fine-tunes it using accurate energies. Both strategies use approximate physical models to expand the information available to the network.

On three benchmark datasets, the first strategy improves baseline neural-network performance by 5–51%, while the second achieves improvements of up to 55%. Combining the strategies yields further gains. These results support using empirical potentials as a source of training knowledge, with accurate quantum-mechanical data still anchoring the learning process.
neurips-2022-injecting-domain-knowledge-.tldr: Two training strategies transfer knowledge from inexpensive empirical atomic potentials to improve neural models trained with limited accurate energy labels.

paragraphs: Optimal transport matches distributions by minimizing a transport cost, but the cheapest matching can sometimes be incorrect for the application. This paper considers settings where a few correct cross-domain correspondences are available as annotated keypoints. It develops a method for using those known matches to guide the remaining transport plan.

KPG-RL combines two forms of guidance. A mask-based constraint preserves the supplied keypoint pairings. A relation-preservation requirement then encourages other points to match in a way that respects their relationships to those keypoints. The keypoints consequently provide both fixed correspondences and a reference structure for matching the rest of the data.

The resulting model can be solved with Sinkhorn's algorithm and can handle distributions represented in different spaces. The authors also incorporate relation preservation into the Kantorovich and Gromov-Wasserstein formulations and extend their model to partial transport. Experiments in heterogeneous domain adaptation verify the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to make limited correspondence annotations influence the broader matching problem, including when direct comparison across representation spaces is difficult.
neurips-2022-keypoint-guided-optimal-tra.tldr: KPG-RL guides optimal transport with known keypoint matches and preserved relationships to those keypoints, including across different representation spaces.

paragraphs: Complex physical systems can often be understood as interacting subsystems. This paper brings that modular viewpoint to learned simulation of homogeneous multibody systems. Rather than learning only a single complete-system model, the framework learns an individual dynamical subsystem as a reusable neural ordinary differential equation module.

To simulate a complete system, the modules exchange messages across space and time. This combines the interaction structure of graph neural networks with continuous-time learned dynamics. An arbitrary number of modules can be assembled with different coupling patterns, allowing the same framework to represent a variety of system configurations.

Experiments show that message passing coordinates the modules over time and supports accurate predictions. In some cases, the learned modules generalize to new configurations without additional training. When adaptation is needed, transferring the models requires less data and training effort than learning from scratch. These findings support modularity as a useful design principle for learned simulation, while keeping the zero-shot claim specific to the cases where it was observed.
neurips-2022-learning-modular-simulation.tldr: Reusable neural dynamics modules communicate through message passing to simulate coupled systems and reduce the effort needed to adapt to new configurations.

paragraphs: Multilingual fine-tuning uses several source languages to prepare a pretrained language model for tasks in target languages without target-language training examples. The paper identifies a difficulty in this process: adapting to the source languages can erase cross-language knowledge acquired during pretraining. That forgetting can reduce zero-shot performance on the target languages.

Less-forgetting Multilingual Fine-tuning reformulates adaptation as constrained optimization. Its objective is to minimize forgetting, while its constraints require reducing the fine-tuning loss. This gives knowledge retention an explicit role in the optimization problem while preserving the requirement to learn the downstream task.

The authors show that the proposed method can achieve Pareto stationarity, a theoretical property concerning the balance among competing objectives. Experiments on named entity recognition, question answering, and natural language inference support the analysis and show superior zero-shot performance. The findings connect better transfer to managing what fine-tuning preserves, as well as what it learns. They support treating cross-language knowledge retention as a central part of multilingual adaptation.
neurips-2022-less-forgetting-multi-lingu.tldr: LF-MLF explicitly minimizes forgetting during multilingual fine-tuning to improve zero-shot performance on target languages.

paragraphs: Coverage control asks multiple agents to position themselves so that they collectively cover an important spatial density. The problem becomes harder when that density is initially unknown and some locations may be unsafe under constraints that are also unknown. The agents must learn where to go while accounting for both coverage and safety.

The authors introduce a conditionally linear, submodular coverage function that makes theoretical analysis possible. Building on that structure, MacOpt balances exploring the environment with using current knowledge to improve coverage. The paper proves sublinear regret for this algorithm, establishing a long-run guarantee for its handling of partial information.

SafeMac extends the approach by adapting single-agent safe-exploration results to multiple agents. The authors prove finite-time near-optimal coverage together with safety guarantees in their analyzed setting. Evaluations include synthetic and real problems, with a biodiversity-monitoring task involving safety constraints where SafeMac outperforms competing methods. The contribution links learning an unknown coverage objective with safe exploration, rather than assuming either the important locations or the safe regions are already fully known.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-multi-agent-le.tldr: MacOpt and SafeMac learn unknown coverage objectives, with SafeMac providing finite-time near-optimal coverage and safety guarantees in the analyzed setting.

paragraphs: A changing network may undergo shifts whose timing is important to identify, even when its information must remain private. This paper studies locating those change points in sequences of networks under local differential privacy. It considers both node-level and edge-level privacy constraints, extending analysis beyond static private networks.

The authors derive signal-to-noise conditions that describe when consistent localization is possible and identify a phase transition in those conditions. They also provide polynomial-time algorithms. These results quantify how privacy changes the statistical information required to find a shift, including a different dependence on network sparsity from the corresponding non-private problem.

Under edge-level local privacy, the algorithms achieve optimal performance up to logarithmic factors. Under node-level local privacy, the upper and lower bounds do not match, leaving the precise difficulty unresolved. This distinction is part of the paper's contribution: it gives a sharp characterization for edge privacy while exposing an open question for node privacy. The findings connect the chosen privacy constraint to both achievable localization accuracy and the strength of available guarantees.
neurips-2022-network-change-point-locali.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy costs in network change-point localization, obtaining near-optimal edge-private algorithms while leaving a gap for node privacy.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from data collected by a behavior policy. This paper studies how much data are needed to reach a target accuracy, epsilon, when the available data sufficiently cover an optimal policy. The coverage assumption is expressed through an upper bound on the density ratio between the optimal and behavior policies.

Previous results give a sample-complexity rate proportional to 1/epsilon squared under this single-policy coverage assumption, with matching worst-case optimality. The authors show that an additional gap in the optimal Q-function allows a faster 1/epsilon rate under the same coverage assumption. The gap supplies extra problem structure beyond what the general worst-case analysis assumes.

With a stronger uniform single-policy coverage assumption, the paper further improves the dependence on epsilon to a constant. This is a statement about accuracy dependence under the stated assumptions, not a claim that data are unnecessary. Nearly matching lower bounds accompany the upper bounds. Together, the results show how value gaps and the strength of coverage can substantially change the statistical difficulty of offline learning.
neurips-2022-on-gap-dependent-bounds-for.tldr: A gap in the optimal Q-function improves offline reinforcement-learning sample-complexity rates under coverage assumptions, with stronger coverage enabling constant dependence on target accuracy.

paragraphs: A crystal can be represented by a unit cell that repeats through three-dimensional space. Learning from this representation requires distinguishing physical structure from arbitrary choices about where the cell begins and ends. Shifting those boundaries should not change the representation, but meaningful differences in repeating lattice patterns must still be captured.

The paper introduces Matformer, a transformer architecture for periodic graphs. It is designed to preserve periodic invariance while explicitly representing repetition. Its mechanism uses geometric distances between copies of the same atoms in neighboring cells, allowing the model to encode the repeating structure efficiently.

Across multiple common benchmark datasets, Matformer consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines. The reported results also demonstrate the importance of both periodic invariance and explicit repetition encoding. These findings support a representation tailored to crystals' repeating geometry: it should avoid sensitivity to artificial cell boundaries while retaining information that distinguishes different materials. The contribution is an architecture that incorporates these two requirements directly into crystal-property prediction.
neurips-2022-periodic-graph-transformers.tldr: Matformer encodes crystal repetition while remaining invariant to artificial unit-cell boundaries, improving property prediction on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Some deployed models must adapt as class definitions evolve while retaining accuracy on earlier definitions. Fraud detection provides one motivation, because new schemes continually change what the model must recognize. The paper names this problem Learning with Dynamic Definition and shows substantial forgetting in models including Vision Transformer and RoBERTa.

Retraining on all available data can address updates, but the authors identify its inefficiency as a barrier to real-time and on-device learning. Their alternative, RIDDLE, uses hashing to create a sparse association between samples and relevant parameters. This structure is designed to handle evolving definitions while limiting the knowledge disrupted by updates.

The paper proves that RIDDLE is a universal function approximator and provides a theoretical bound on knowledge lost during updating. On vision and language tasks with changing class definitions, it improves performance on the original dataset by up to 30% over baselines while remaining competitive on the update dataset. The results link selective parameter involvement with retaining prior knowledge, alongside evidence that the model can still learn the updated definitions.
neurips-2022-retaining-knowledge-for-lea.tldr: RIDDLE uses hash-based sparse parameter associations to learn evolving class definitions while bounding knowledge loss and improving retention in experiments.

paragraphs: Connecting discrete values with continuous distributions often requires choosing how continuous space is divided into discrete regions. This paper learns those boundaries directly through a geometric partition, or tessellation. The method retains exact likelihood evaluation, so the learned mapping comes with a way to compute probabilities.

The construction places normalizing flows on convex polytopes using a continuous, invertible mapping with an efficiently computed log-determinant Jacobian. In the discrete-to-continuous direction, Voronoi dequantization learns multidimensional region boundaries. The positions of those boundaries and the distances between regions can represent useful structural relationships among discrete values.

In the other direction, the authors introduce a Voronoi mixture model whose likelihood-evaluation cost is nearly constant as the number of mixture components grows. Experiments report improvements over existing methods across several structured data modalities. The contribution combines learnable geometry with tractable probability calculations: the partition itself becomes part of the model, and the same construction supports both dequantization and efficient mixture modeling.
neurips-2022-semi-discrete-normalizing-f.tldr: Learned geometric partitions connect discrete and continuous distributions while supporting exact likelihoods and efficient mixture evaluation.

paragraphs: Many collections, such as the items in an e-commerce order, are naturally treated as sets rather than ordered sequences. This paper proposes a general method for converting a maximum-likelihood sequence generator into a set generator. The resulting model can evaluate the probability or utility of a set.

Learning the converted model creates a computational challenge, which the authors address with importance sampling. They present GRU2Set as an implementation based on a GRU sequence model and introduce SetNN to obtain representations that are invariant to permutations. They also propose a size-bias technique, motivated by the idea that smaller sets are usually easier to learn, to improve distribution quality measured by L1 distance.

Experiments on TMALL and HKTVMALL order data show better learned set distributions than the evaluated baselines. The size-bias technique improves distribution quality across the models used in the experiments. Learning such order distributions can support operational decisions, including inventory arrangement for faster delivery. The contribution therefore connects sequence-modeling tools with probability estimation for unordered collections.
neurips-2022-sequence-to-set-generative-.tldr: A sequence-to-set framework adapts sequence generators to unordered collections and improves e-commerce order-distribution learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Phylogenetic inference estimates relationships represented as trees, including relationships relevant to single-cell medical research. The number of possible trees grows exponentially, making Bayesian inference difficult. The paper identifies obstacles in both local-search-based Markov chain Monte Carlo methods and variational methods that rely on costly automatic differentiation.

VaiPhy performs approximate posterior inference in an augmented tree space using coordinate-ascent updates instead of automatic differentiation. It combines these updates with two sampling schemes. SLANTIS proposes tree topologies in the augmented space, while the JC sampler draws branch lengths directly from the Jukes-Cantor model. Together, these components address the discrete tree structure and its branch-length parameters.

On real data, VaiPhy produces marginal log-likelihood estimates comparable to state-of-the-art methods while running considerably faster. The authors evaluate density estimation and runtime and also examine the reproducibility of the baselines. The stated result is a favorable balance between inference quality and computation: the method avoids a costly optimization mechanism without sacrificing the reported quality of marginal likelihood estimates.
neurips-2022-vaiphy-a-variational-infere.tldr: VaiPhy combines coordinate-ascent updates with specialized tree and branch-length samplers to accelerate approximate Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

paragraphs: Some tasks require an agent to succeed once, without a restart or human intervention, while facing unfamiliar conditions. This paper formalizes that setting as single-life reinforcement learning. The agent may draw on previous experience, but it must complete the new task within one episode while adapting to novelty.

The authors find that methods designed for standard episodic reinforcement learning often struggle to recover after entering states outside their prior experience. They propose Q-weighted adversarial learning, or QWALE, to address this difficulty. Its distribution-matching strategy uses prior experience as guidance when the agent encounters new situations, with recovery playing a central role in eventual task completion.

Across several single-life continuous-control problems, methods based on the proposed formulation are reported to be 20–60% more successful because they recover more quickly from novel states. These findings support studying adaptation through success within a single uninterrupted attempt. The contribution includes both a problem formulation for that requirement and an algorithm designed around using existing experience to navigate unfamiliar conditions.
neurips-2022-you-only-live-once-single-l.tldr: Single-life reinforcement learning studies success within one uninterrupted attempt, and QWALE uses prior experience to improve recovery from novel states.
